Items.Authors: Julien Storm, Gert Raskin, Louis Storm, Bart Vandenbussche, Hugues Sana, Dirk Vandepitte, Leonardo Peri, Sibo Van Gool, Pierre Royer, Maddalena Reggiani, Camille Pirat, Jorg Versluys, Mathijs Arts
Items.Title: Design, assembly, and alignment strategy of the CubeSpec Cassegrain Telescope
Items.Abstract: CubeSpec is a 12U CubeSat mission designed to demonstrate high-resolution spectroscopy from a compact platform. The mission is now in construction phase with launch readiness early 2027. We present the design, assembly and alignment strategy, of the compact off-axis CubeSpec Cassegrain telescope, feeding the CubeSpec high resolution echelle slit spectrograph. The telescope is installed in a 12U CubeSat and features a parabolic primary mirror (M1) and hyperbolic secondary mirror (M2), achieving a focal length of 1600 mm (F/8.33 - F/17) with a rectangular entrance aperture (94×192 mm) to maximize light collection. The off-axis configuration eliminates central obscuration and simplifies mechanical mounting.

Items.Authors: Jón E. Guðmundsson, Thomas J. Gascard, Miranda Eiben, Rustam Balafendiev, Ashesh Khatua, Xiaodong Ren, Eve Vavagiakis
Items.Title: Design, assembly, and initial test results of a cryostat for holographic testing of microwave telescopes
Items.Abstract: We present the design, assembly, and initial test results of a 4-Kelvin cryostat developed for characterization of the Taurus balloon-borne microwave telescopes. The cylindrical cryostat, approximately 1.5 m in diameter and 1.0 m in length, consists of three thermal stages: a 300-K vacuum vessel, a 40-K radiation shield, and a 4-K cold stage. The two cryogenic stages, each mechanically supported by six thermally isolating G10 flexures, are cooled by a Bluefors PT420 pulse-tube cryocooler. The cryostat provides sufficient volume to perform holographic measurements of the full three-lens refractor optical systems designed for the Taurus experiment as well as other refracting systems for the cosmic microwave background. We discuss thermal and mechanical design aspects and present early results from cryogenic testing. The system represents the first cryostat ever built in Iceland.

Items.Authors: Jacob Payne, Casey T. DeRoo
Items.Title: Designing compact x-ray optics with multilayer coatings for pulsar-informed navigation
Items.Abstract: Millisecond pulsars exhibit predictable long-term stability, comparable to atomic clocks, and can serve as natural beacons for autonomous position and timing systems. Multi-layer coatings can give flexibility to telescope geometries by providing reflective efficiency greater than 20% at grazing incidence angles greater than 3 degrees, and with Bragg reflection at 45 degrees. We present the results from phase-resolved spectral analysis of NICER measurements for a set of millisecond pulsars that are prime candidates for Pulsar-informed Navigation (PIN). This analysis identifies the energy bands to enhance the signal to noise ratio of the pulsed emission. Customized multi-layer coatings can be designed to reflect photons at this energy across a wider range of grazing incidence angles, enabling shorter focal lengths for more compact telescopes. We discuss the design implications of the phase-resolved spectra on the optics and multi-layer coatings for a PIN instrument.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Matthijs Mars, Louis Desdoigts, Jared R. Males, Joseph D. Long, Rico Landman, Olivier Guyon, Sandrine Juillard
Items.Title: Detecting rocky exoplanets within minutes with the next generation of Extremely Large Telescopes and telemetry-based post-processing
Items.Abstract: Every high-contrast imaging system needs to use post-processing to remove residual starlight from its measurement. Many algorithms lose performance at close separations due to the small diversities. We propose to use telemetry-based post-processing (TDI) where we use the information of all wavefront sensors in the system together with the science instrument to predict the stellar speckles. These can then be subtracted from the actual measurement. This approach reaches the photon noise limits at optimal efficiency without any required prior knowledge of the exoplanet. An end-to-end model is used to predict the performance of the upcoming extremely large telescopes. We will discuss the results and show that the ELTs can characterize many nearby exoplanet within minutes and that they could potentially achieve similar performance as space-based high-contrast imaging systems.

Items.Authors: Eckhart A. Spalding, Thomas Birbacher, Felix Dannert, Adrian Glauser, Jonah Hansen, Maximilian Kirchhoff, Sascha Quanz
Items.Title: Detector considerations for the LIFE mission
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) is a formation-flying mission for enabling the detection and characterization of potentially dozens of Earth-sized planets at thermal infrared wavelengths. The mission will need to sieve science signals which are many orders of magnitude fainter than competing systematics, and the science detector itself will contribute potentially highly variable noise terms. We present requirements for detector read noise, quantum efficiency, and other detector characteristics, for observations of potential LIFE targets. We compare mission needs with detectors available on the market, or in development, and include a discussion of the ramifications on the surrounding mission design. Expected high-level noise budgets and predicted planet yields based on detector type are presented, and we conclude with a discussion of the most relevant future avenues in detector development and eventual integration.

Items.Authors: Timothy Butterley, David Barr, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Sofia Dimoudi, Kathryn Hartley, Linn Htat Lu, Luke Johnson, Timothy Morris, Emily Ronson, Dirk Schmidt, Jurgen Schmoll
Items.Title: Determination of the atmospheric turbulence profile from image distortions in a wide field solar wavefront sensor
Items.Abstract: Ground based solar telescopes require multi conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) to achieve the best possible resolution, which in turn requires detailed knowledge of the atmospheric turbulence profile. The profile can be measured using a solar version of the slope detection and ranging (SLODAR) technique, using a wide field Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (WFS) that measures wavefront slopes by tracking image motion. As well as overall motion, subaperture images also contain distortions due to differential tip/tilt variations. Usually these are regarded as a noise source but we propose to measure them in order to derive extra information about high altitude turbulence and hence improve the profile resolution. We present a method of measuring WFS image distortions using machine learning, demonstrate how turbulence profiles can be derived from these measurements. We apply this method to experimental data from the Nēnē solar SLODAR turbulence profiling instrument on the DKIST telescope.

Items.Authors: David R. Jenkins, Daniel Jodlbauer, Pierre Haguenauer, Dietrich Pescoller, Christian Patauner, Felipe Pedreros Bustos
Items.Title: Developing and operating AO RTC software for LGS R&D
Items.Abstract: Artic (Advanced Real-Time Instrument Controller) has been developed to operate the ESO/ESA CaNaPy LGS AO R&D experiment and the Microgate led ALASCA project. It has enabled the commissioning of the AO WFSs, real-time acquisition of AO telemetry data and it has been successful in running the AO operations of CaNaPy and ALASCA. It is under continual ongoing development to implement experimental operating modes. Artic consists of core real-time control processes along with high level scripting and GUI control interfaces which communicate through shared memory structures. We present a description of the Artic software, an overview of the results it has achieved so far and a look into the future experiments that will be enabled by the Artic software.

Items.Authors: Rianne Plantenga, Hendrik M. Veen, Antonius H. M. Coppens, Daniela Perez Capelo, Pieter J. de Visser
Items.Title: Developing Hf-NbTiN hybrid Kinetic Inductance Detectors for low light level observations
Items.Abstract: Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) are promising candidates for astronomical studies with low photon intensity, like exoplanet spectroscopy, due to their high sensitivity, and the fact that they retain the color information of the photons they detect. Hybrid detector designs with high-Tc NbTiN capacitors and readout circuitry, combined with low-Tc inductors from Al or b-Ta have been demonstrated to effectively increase sensitivity by concentrating quasiparticles in the most sensitive part of the detector. However a resolving power R>100 required for Habitable Worlds Observatory is not yet achieved.    Devices with Hafnium as low-Tc inductors are predicted to have a higher energy resolution. Here we show the progress in developing Hf-NbTiN hybrid KIDs and first measurements on such device. We find an average internal quality factor of 4.76E5 at low microwave power and a surprisingly low bifurcation threshold. We also show the first measurements on the energy resolution of these devices.

Items.Authors: Phillip J. Wise, Stephen Bongiorno
Items.Title: Development and testing of a circular whiffle tree fixture for supporting full-shell x-ray optics during x-ray tests
Items.Abstract: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) produces full-shell replicated X-ray optics for scientific applications. Testing single, unmounted full-shell optics in an X-ray beamline is an important part of the development process. The intentionally thin optics distort significantly under their own self-gravity when mounted horizontally in a beamline. It is therefore necessary to develop methods for holding them in a minimally stressed, natural state. We have developed a new mounting solution that utilizes a circular whiffle-tree to apply azimuthally varying force on the exterior of the shell to minimize deformation. The circular whiffle is advantageous in that it allows for quick mounting of shells, may reduce gravity deformation compared to existing solutions, and is relatively low cost. This paper describes the design, manufacture, and testing of the circular wiffle and compares it to mounting methods currently used in MSFC’s 100-meter x-ray beamline.

Items.Authors: Ryuji Kondo, Shen Hsien-Chieh, Makoto Arimoto, Tatsuro Kanenaga, Hiro Otsuka, Daisuke Yonetoku, Shutaro Ueda, Tatsuya Sawano, Junko Hiraga, Takanori Sakamoto, Hiroshi Nakajima, Hiroshi Tomida, Akihiro Doi, Hideo Matsuhara, Robert Hartmann, Lothar Strüder
Items.Title: Development and X-ray detection demonstration of pnCCD driver and readout system for future satellite mission HiZ-GUNDAM
Items.Abstract: Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic explosions in the universe, releasing 10^52–10^54 erg of energy over durations ranging from several tens of milliseconds to several hundred seconds. HiZ-GUNDAM is a satellite mission designed to explore the early universe using GRBs as probes. Its wide-field X-ray monitor, EAGLE, consists of Lobster Eye Optics and pnCCD as focal-plane detectors. We have developed a pnCCD drive and readout system using custom electronic boards. We characterized the front-end ASIC and then connected a pnCCD image sensor (12.7 × 25.3 mm², 450 µm depletion, 132 µm pixels). We obtained dark frames, Fe-55 X-ray–irradiated images showing spot-like events and Mn-Kα/Kβ line structures and charged-particle events from an Sr-90 source. We also collected data at several temperatures (–20 to 0 °C). In this presentation, we report on the current status of pnCCD drive experiments performed with the constructed readout system.

Items.Authors: Hiroomi Hata, Naoki Isobe, Yasumasa Yamasaki, Takeru Matsumoto, Satoru Iguchi
Items.Title: Development of a foreground model for detecting global signals of the neutral hydrogen 21 cm line from the cosmic dark ages
Items.Abstract: The TSUKUYOMI is a project planning to construct decameter antenna system on the Moon to observe radio waves below 55MHz with the goal of verifying the standard cosmology by exploring the Cosmic Dark Ages. It is important and critical to calibrate the foreground emission from the Milky Way and other radio sources and the telescope instrument noises which are much larger than this absorption amount, aiming to detect the neutral hydrogen 21cm line global signal.  Here we developed a software tool to convolve the Milky Way emission with beam pattern of a dipole antenna on the Moon. This talk will introduce our newly developed tool and discuss the time dependence and frequency response of the expected spectrum calculated with this tool. We also explore the possibility of detecting the global signal of neutral hydrogen 21cm line hidden in the foreground emission.

Items.Authors: Pratyush Rajaure, Ankit Sangroula, Shivaram Phuyal, Birat Prasad Subedi, Utsav Kandel, Srishant Dhakal, Rishi Ram Paudel, Ramesh Koirala, Damodar Pokhrel, Lelin Adhikari, Nin Waam Rai, Hari Ram Shrestha, Suresh Kumar Dhungel
Items.Title: Development of a low-cost observatory-grade telescope using local engineering in Nepal
Items.Abstract: We present the development of a 16-inch optical telescope designed and manufactured entirely by local engineering expertise in Nepal. The project aims to demonstrate that high-quality astronomical instruments can be constructed using regional materials, indigenous technical capability, and cost-effective fabrication processes. In doing so, we seek to establish a sustainable model for the development of research infrastructure in countries with emerging scientific communities.

Items.Authors: Fernando Gutierrez Cabrera, Luis Carlos Alvarez Nuñez, Alejando Farah Simon, Jose Leonardo Garces Medina, Arturo Renteria Lartundo, Erika Maria Benitez Lizaola
Items.Title: Development of a monitor for estimating induced seeing at the National Astronomical Observatory of Tonantzintla
Items.Abstract: The image quality obtained from telescopes can be affected not only by the external atmosphere but also by turbulence generated within the dome by thermal gradients and airflow. At the National Astronomical Observatory in Tonantzintla (OANTON), as in most astronomical facilities, available measurements are limited to external atmospheric seeing, so there is no quantitative information on the contribution of internal turbulence. To address this gap, we propose the design and installation of a monitoring system that uses a collimated beam propagated along an internal path parallel to the stellar optical path, allowing the measurement of fluctuations resulting from turbulence within the dome. This instrument will provide direct and continuous measurements of air behavior inside the telescope and will allow the evaluation of the impact of thermal and ventilation conditions on image quality.

Items.Authors: Carla J. Baldovin Saveedra, Mark Ruiter, Paulus Kruger, Boudewijn Hut
Items.Title: Development of a new fronted for the LOFAR telescope: decision making process during product development
Items.Abstract: This contribution reports on the challenges and success encountered during the development of a new frontend deployed in the High Band Antennas of the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), the most sensitive radio telescope operating since 2010 at the lowest frequencies observable from Earth (10-250 MHz).     The product delivered presents several improvements: increased linearity, beamformer accuracy, easier manufacturability, and robustness due to improved potting. While production costs were kept similar to the previous version.     I will reflect on the project since its inception; including the decision-making process at management level that balanced external stakeholder expectations and internal operational needs and how those decisions impacted the execution of the project.

Items.Authors: Kanaho Okamoto, Tatsuya Sawano, Yusuke Munakata, Atsushi Takada, Shinya Sonoda, Mitsuru Abe, Kai Matsunaga, Soma Deguchi, Taiyo Sato, Sana Okumura, Haruki Onoda, Hiroki Yoneda, Takeshi Nakamori, Haruki Iiyama, Dai Yaegashi, Shun Suzuki, Yoshitaka Mizumura, Masaki Morita, Tomohiko Oka, Kenji Hamaguchi, Junko Kushida, Kyoshi Nishijima, Shunsuke Kurosawa, Kentaro Miuchi, Toru Tanimori
Items.Title: Development of an anticoincidence scintillation detector for SMILE-3 to investigate negative spectral lags in GRBs
Items.Abstract: Observations in the MeV energy band are a key step to investigate the origin of the diverse spectral lags in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The SMILE-3 experiment is designed to survey this energy range using an Electron-Tracking Compton Camera (ETCC). We have developed a lightweight, compact balloon-borne anticoincidence scintillation detector capable of both rejecting cosmic-ray events and detecting low-energy GRBs. The detector employs a plastic scintillator, silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), and readout electronics. We present the performance of the developed electronics and its GRB detection capability evaluated by sensitivity calculations.

Items.Authors: Vicente Westerhout, Maximiliano Torres, Esteban Vera
Items.Title: Development of an event-based Shack-Hartmann image motion monitor
Items.Abstract: Turbulence profiling is of great use in adaptive optics for astronomy, space situational awareness and free-space optical communications. For this reason, efforts in upgrading the replicability and mobility requirements of turbulence profilers is needed. In this work, a Shack-Hartmann image motion monitor using an event-based camera is implemented to leverage the high temporal resolution, low power consumption and low processing load of neuromorphic devices. This complies with the replicability and mobility requirements by using only components-of-the-shelf. Comparisons of atmospheric measurements between our system and the traditional SHIMM system are provided for the SEETRUE optical ground station in Valparaiso, Chile.

Items.Authors: Nabin Poudyal, Paul Ray, Eric Wulf, Wayne Baumgartner, Gianluigi De Geronimo, Jarred Roberts, Wesley Hodge, Sukanya Chakrabarti, Peter Jenke
Items.Title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation.
Items.Abstract: We develop an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large-area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC, and achieve a noise performance of 5 e⁻ ENC as a function of input charge, input capacitance, and shaping time. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful DAQ system integration.

Items.Authors: Chao-Te Li, Jen-Chieh Cheng, Chung-Cheng Chen, Pai-An Chen, Ta-Shun Wei, Chin-Ting Ho, Ue-Li Pen
Items.Title: Development of differential transmission for BURSTT
Items.Abstract: Bustling Universe Radio Survey Telescope in Taiwan (BURSTT) aims to build a phased array with a large field of view to detect and localize fast radio bursts (FRBs) in the local universe. Phase I of BURSTT includes a main array with 256 antennas and 2 outrigger stations with 64 antennas around Taiwan. For phase I, we used off-the-shelf components to quickly set up the array. An FRB was detected with BURSTT-256 in July 2025, which verifies the array design. As phase I is completed, to cope with phase II with much larger arrays, we developed modules with integrated circuits. Since antennas, optical fiber transmission, and Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC) are essentially differential, to avoid the use of baluns and take advantage of the development of telecommunication technologies, we adopted differential or balanced transmission. This article describes the design and testing of various differential modules that we developed.

Items.Authors: Deli Geng, Kieran O'Brien, David Barr, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Sofia Dimoudi, James Gill-Fleming, Aurelie Magniez
Items.Title: Development of Dual Feedline MKIDs Readout Based on RFSoC 4x2 Board
Items.Abstract: The RFSoC FPGA with RF ADC/DAC and system level processor integrated on a single chip has been well used in MKIDs readout systems. For example, the MazinLab at UCSB developed an open source pipeline processing the MKIDs readout signal from the ADC to produce the photon pulse detection. Based on UCSB’s work, the MKIDs team at Durham University further added a phase stream interface to connect GPU for the real-time pulse analysis.     In fact, the RFSoC FPGA has multiple on-chip RF ADC/DAC resources capable to support more than one readout feedline. A dual feedline design would almost half the cost per detector on the FPGA side.     The RFSoC 4x2 board, although competitive with lower cost, has reduced number of the RF ADC/DAC external connections, which is not enough for two feedlines by the common I/Q RF based MKIDs readout. This presentation shows a way to connect two feedlines with a single RFSoC 4x2 board. Both the RF interface hardware and firmware design will be discussed.

Items.Authors: Diane Hascall, Margaux Lopez, Felipe Bustos, Matthew Rumore, Mostafa Lutfi, Holger Drass, Travis Lange, David Cabrera, Iain Goodenow, Eduardo Serrano, Jeff Barr, Charles Claver
Items.Title: Development of the computerized maintenance management system for the Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Rubin Observatory has transitioned from construction into operations, prompting the need for robust tracking of maintenance activities essential to maintaining peak performance. The LSST Camera, a complex system and the observatory’s sole instrument, has been a major component for developing Rubin’s new Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS). Beyond scheduling tasks, the CMMS must track assets, catalog inventory, and support observatory-specific workflows, requiring significant customization and integration with existing planning tools. LSST Camera maintenance needs—including routine calendar-based tasks and data-driven, condition-based activities informed by the Engineering Facilities Database (EFD)—provide key inputs for this development. This paper presents the current status of CMMS design, customization efforts, and camera-related activities that informed those decisions.

Items.Authors: Hironori Matsumoto, Hidetoshi Sakamoto, Kaito Murakami, Takuya Hosobata, Hisamitsu Awaki, Haruki Kuramoto, Shin-ya Morita, Sayana Takatsuka, Masahiro Takeda, Yutaka Yamagata
Items.Title: Development of the light-weight X-ray Wolter-I mirror using carbon fiber reinforced plastic and ultra-precision machining technology
Items.Abstract: Lightweight X-ray mirrors with high angular resolution and a large effective area are essential for clarifying the coevolution of galaxies and black holes. To realize such mirrors, we are developing X-ray optics using carbon fiber–reinforced plastic (CFRP), a light yet strong material that can be formed into various shapes. However,CFRP exhibits a finely textured surface pattern known as print-through, which makes the surface too rough for X-ray reflection. To mitigate print-through, we developed a method to form a thin amorphous NiP layer on the CFRP surface. The NiP layer is then finished using ultra-precision machining to achieve the surface smoothness required for X-ray reflection. We are currently developing a Wolter-I CFRP mirror shell. The mirror shell has an aperture diameter of 100 mm, a focal length of 2000 mm, and a segment length of 100 mm for both the parabolic and hyperbolic sections. We will present the current status of this mirror development.

Items.Authors: Mitsuyoshi Yamagishi, Shigeyuki Sako, Masahiro Konishi, Hiroaki Sameshima, Natsuko Kato, Yuki Mori, Sohei Kondo, Takashi Miyata, Kotaro Kohno, Kentaro Motohara, Takeo Minezaki, Fumi Egusa, Itsuki Sakon, Hidenori Takahashi, Takafumi Kamizuka, Kazuya Matsubayashi, Kana Morokuma-Matsui, Masataka Imai, Takashi Horiuchi, Yuki Hirao, Yuzuru Yoshii
Items.Title: Development of the summit information system for the TAO 6.5m telescope
Items.Abstract: Real-time monitoring of site conditions is crucial to conduct observations safely. Such monitoring is, however, challenging for the TAO 6.5m telescope, which is located at Co. Chajnantor, Chile, with altitude of 5640m above sea level. By overcoming difficulties due to harsh environment of this site, we are developing a summit information system to obtain environmental data at the observation site and deliver them to observers. Up to date, we have achieved real-time monitoring of weather and web-camera data at the summit from anywhere in the world. In this presentation, we overview the current components of the summit information system and future plans.

Items.Authors: Yusuke Yoshida, Kazuki Ampuku, Koki Sakuta, Makoto Yoshihara, Keitoku Yoshihira, Ryoma Tanaka, Tetsuo Kano, Naoki Ishida, Wataru Kato, Yoshitaka Inoue, Keisuke Tamura, Takashi Okajima, Kikuko Miyata, Noriyuki Narukage, Gota Yamaguchi, Shutaro Mohri, Satoru Egawa, Hiroto Motoyama, Takehiro Kume, Yusuke Matsuzawa, Yoichi Imamura, Takahiro Saito, Kentaro Hiraguri, Hirokazu Hashizume, Hidekazu Mimura, Ikuyuki Mitsuishi
Items.Title: Development of X-ray optics for the solar flare sounding rocket FOXSI-5
Items.Abstract: We have been developing X-ray optics for the 5th Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager (FOXSI-5), a Japan–U.S. joint solar sounding rocket experiment scheduled for launch in April 2026, aimed at revealing particle acceleration and plasma heating mechanisms in solar flares. The previous mission, FOXSI-4, achieved the world's first X-ray imaging and spectroscopic observation of a solar flare using our soft and hard X-ray optics. For FOXSI-5, we have prepared the reused hard X-ray optics and a newly fabricated soft X-ray optics. As a result of evaluation of the soft X-ray optics, we obtained the imaging performance of FWHM ~ 0.3 arcsec and HPD ~ 9 arcsec at 12 keV, and the effective area of ~ 15 mm^2 for on-axis rays, achieving one of the highest angular resolutions in the FOXSI series. We will report the latest status of our X-ray optics, which is a key to FOXSI-5.

Items.Authors: Dehua Yang, Xin He, Xiaofei Li, Hua Bai, Bo Li, Fanghua Jiang, Shihai Yang, Dongsheng Niu, Lingzhe Xu, Shouwei Hu, Yongjun Liang, Yuefei Wang, Xiang Jiang
Items.Title: Development status of the 4-m segmented Jiaotong University Spectroscopic Telescope (JUST)
Items.Abstract: We present the current engineering development status of the Jiaotong University Spectroscopic Telescope (JUST), a 4-meter class optical telescope designed for high-efficiency spectral surveys and time-domain astronomy. JUST utilizes a segmented primary mirror architecture delivering competitive spectroscopic capabilities. This paper details the transition from conceptual design to the critical design and prototyping phases of the telescope structure systems.  The primary mirror (M1) consists of 18 hexagonal segments We report on the structural optimization of the Segment Support Assembly, the alt-azimuth mount design, and the site infrastructure development at the Lenghu observing station. The paper also describes the mechanical implementation of the Active Optics System using edge sensors and a Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor.

Items.Authors: Akihiro Fujie, Shota Narasaki, Yuto Owaki, Misaki Miyake, Junji Takaki, Tomoya Hattori, Koji Hirose, Teppe Ikezaki, Akihiro Ando, Deprez Maxime, Claire Lamour, Yukio Katsukawa, Yusuke Kawabata, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Naoki Kohara, Yoshinori Suematsu, Fumihiro Uraguchi, Hirohisa Hara, Kota Miyoshi, Hideki Kato, Toshifumi Shimizu
Items.Title: Development status of the primary mirror and pre-coating optical measurement results for the SOLAR-C EUVST
Items.Abstract: This report details the development status of the engineering model (EM) and flight model (FM) of the primary mirror for the SOLAR-C EUV Spectroscopic Telescope (EUVST), including measurements of surface figure error (SFE) with the mirror support mechanism. A bipod-based support with leaf springs was designed and implemented to minimize mirror deformation caused by mechanical and thermal loading. The validation with the EM primary mirror demonstrated that the predicted and measured astigmatism and coma abberations agreed well, confirming the robustness of the mirror support design. For the FM mirror, gravity-reversal measurements verified that the mirror’s SFE met the optical specifications.

Items.Authors: Ian Czekala, Jeff Jennings, Brianna Zawadzki, Kadri Nizam, Ryan Loomis
Items.Title: Differentiable models for radio astronomy interferometer calibration and image synthesis
Items.Abstract: Astronomical radio interferometers achieve exquisite angular resolution by cross-correlating signals from a cosmic source simultaneously observed by distant pairs of antennas to produce a Fourier-type measurement called a visibility. Here we describe the implementation of a feed-forward modeling approach to synthesize scientific images from interferometric visibility datasets, built using the radio interferometric measurement equation and the autodifferentiable machine learning framework PyTorch. Neural network components provide a rich set of modular and composable building blocks that can be used to express the physical relationships between latent model parameters and observed data, including parameters which might otherwise be restricted to a one-time calibration procedure prior to image synthesis. Industry-grade optimizers make it straightforward to simultaneously solve for the synthesized image and calibration parameters using stochastic gradient descent.

Items.Authors: Stephanie S. Guzman, James Hoag
Items.Title: Discovering the need for dedicated CMMS support for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: A CMMS (Computerized Maintenance Management System) is a type of software that helps companies keep track of and organize maintenance work, track and monitor assets, control inventory, document procedures, and generate relevant reporting data.  In 2024, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope was faced with the task of migrating from a discontinued CMMS platform. During the process of preparing for the migration, inconsistencies among how staff members within different departments use the CMMS became apparent. The Inouye had roughly 30 employees that regularly used the CMMS. This team was made up of technicians, engineers, and supervisors, each of whom had different needs of what they got out of a CMMS. The need for a dedicated employee with experience in software tool configuration and administration to support an accurate and timely migration, maintain consistency of use, work as a liaison between staff and the vendor, and implement new or underutilized features became apparent.

Items.Authors: Jennifer Studer, Devin Crichton, Thierry Viant, Kavilan Moodley, Keshav Bechoo, Tasmiya Papiah, Cornelius Ungerer, Alexandre Refregier
Items.Title: Dish assembly precision of HIRAX and its impact on intensity mapping systematics
Items.Abstract: The Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment (HIRAX) is a radio interferometer array that is currently being deployed at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO) Square Kilometer Array (SKA) site in South Africa. Its aim is to observe neutral hydrogen (HI) through intensity mapping (IM) in the redshift range of 0.775-2.55. HI IM makes it possible to tomographically probe large, cosmological volumes, enabling constraints on, for example, the dark energy equation of state with its large survey of the southern sky. Systematics are a significant concern in deriving cosmological constraints from HI IM. Instrumental effects therefore need to be carefully controlled and monitored with metrological measurements, in particular the precision of mechanical tolerances in the case of redundant interferometric arrays, such as HIRAX. In this work we present the results and implications of the metrological analysis of the 2025-2026 deployment.

Items.Authors: Miroslav Vulinovic, Pedro Escárate
Items.Title: Documented cases of electromagnetic interference in ground-based optical and infrared observatories
Items.Abstract: Awareness of the detrimental effects of electromagnetic interference (EMI) on radio telescopes has existed for decades. In contrast, optical and infrared observatories have traditionally been considered immune due to the distinct operating principles of their detectors. However, experience has demonstrated that their electronic subsystems, particularly charge-coupled devices (CCD) cameras and infrared detectors readouts, can be vulnerable to EMI. Because CCD cameras and infrared detectors remain at the core of many astronomical instruments, this paper reviews the documented cases of EMI affecting ground-based optical and infrared telescopes. Drawing from more than three decades of technical publications and reports, it identifies recurring EMI sources, coupling mechanisms, and their manifestations in detector performance, along with mitigation strategies and best design practices.

Items.Authors: Vincenzo Della Corte, Fabio Cozzolino, Giacomo Ruggiero, Andrea Longobardo, Carlo Bettanini, Giacomo Colombatti, Alessio Aboudan, Fabrizio Dirri, Laura Inno, Ivano Bertini, Giuseppe Sindoni
Items.Title: Dust Next Generation Sensor : SiPMi based instrument for measuring scattered light from dust in extraterrestrial environment.
Items.Abstract: Analyzing space dust and icy plumes is essential for understanding planetary environments and potential habitability. The Dust Next Generation Sensor advances this field by combining optical detection with impact sensors to retrieve particle dynamics (mass, velocity, trajectory).A key evolution from Rosetta’s GIADA instrument is the Optical Stage, which employs Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) to detect light scattered by $1\text{--}100\,\mu\text{m}$ grains. Uniquely, this system utilizes SiPMs in "intensity mode" rather than standard photon counting. This generates continuous waveforms where amplitude reflects grain size and pulse width indicates velocity. SiPMs provide superior mechanical robustness and radiation hardness, ensuring precise detection in harsh space environments despite potentially increased dark count rates.

Items.Authors: Lodovico Coccato, Stefano Zampieri, Wolfram Freudling, Martino Romaniello, Ashley Barnes, Chiara Spiniello
Items.Title: EDPS GUI: a modern graphical frontend for the ESO Data Processing System.
Items.Abstract: The ESO Data Processing System (EDPS) is a framework designed to execute data reduction pipelines for ESO’s instruments at the La Silla Paranal Observatory. EDPS supports a wide range of use cases, from online data quality control at the telescope to interactive use. It has proven to be adequately robust for large-scale processing, and flexible enough to handle different data types. Each pipeline consists of a series of standalone recipes, aimed at to processing specific type of input data. These recipes require various calibration data. EDPS automates the selection of the input files and schedules the execution of recipes according to a selected reduction cascade. EDPS GUI is a web-based Graphical User Interface for EDPS designed for scientific and interactive use. It provides a modern, flexible and user-friendly interface to run EDPS, including configuring and optimising the creation of datasets, the recipe parameters, and inspecting of the results.

Items.Authors: Mariya Krasteva
Items.Title: Enabling in-situ planetary chirality measurements: toward a space-based vibrational circular dichroism spectro-polarimeter
Items.Abstract: Vibrational Circular Dichroism (VCD), measured through the differential absorption of circularly polarized infrared light, provides structural information inaccessible to classical IR spectroscopy. Although well established in laboratory settings, VCD has never been implemented in space or applied to planetary exploration. We outline early design considerations for a conceptual VCD spectro-polarimeter intended for deployment on planetary landers and assess the enabling optical technologies required to support such measurements. These studies are informed by ongoing VCD measurements on commercial instruments and by CHAIS, our assembled laboratory VCD testbed currently undergoing optimisation. This work defines a pathway toward enabling chiral spectroscopy on future planetary missions.

Items.Authors: Sonny Massahi, Diego Paredes-Sanz, Sara Svendsen, Desiree Ferreira, Arne S. Jegers, Finn Christensen
Items.Title: Enabling next-generation multilayer technology for high-energy X-ray telescopes
Items.Abstract: Nickel-based multilayers hold strong potential to extend the upper energy range of current focusing X-ray telescopes. However, crystalline growth in nickel thin films causes large microroughness, limiting performance of small d-spacing multilayers needed for reflecting X-rays up to ~150 keV. Alloy coatings via thin film deposition address this by reducing nickel layer roughness.    This work employs co-sputtering of copper and nickel to create alloy films with disrupted crystalline lattices. This potentially breaks long-range crystallinity of pure copper and nickel, fostering amorphous/polycrystalline growth and substantially lower surface roughness. Such alloy co-sputtering emerges as an enabling strategy for next-generation high-energy X-ray telescope optics, while also enabling smooth thin films for advanced mirror applications. The analyses will be performed using x-ray reflectometry, diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.

Items.Authors: Matthew C. H. Leung, Colby Jurgenson, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, David Charbonneau
Items.Title: Engineering data reduction and alignment diagnostics for the GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF)
Items.Abstract: The two-dimensional spectrum of a high-resolution, cross-dispersed spectrograph exhibits geometric features that provide crucial information about the instrument’s optical alignment. Observable features such as order tilt, slit image tilt, and blaze peak displacement arise from specific optical misalignment modes, including detector clocking, slit assembly rotation, and grating tilt. We are developing an engineering data reduction and alignment diagnostic framework which maps these geometric features to the underlying misalignment modes, enabling targeted alignment corrections during assembly, integration, and test (AIT).

Items.Authors: Lukas Delaye, Iva Laginja, Pierre Baudoz, Axel Potier, Johan Mazoyer, Raphaël Galicher, Susan Redmond, Alexis Lau, Dan Sirbu, A. J. Eldorado Riggs, Emiel H. Por, Rémi Soummer, Laurent Pueyo
Items.Title: Enhanced wavefront sensing for Roman CGI: alternate probes with flight-like validation
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) on the Roman Space Telescope will be the first space-based system to demonstrate closed-loop focal-plane wavefront sensing and control, a key step towards HWO. Beyond the baseline Hybrid Lyot Coronagraph, “enhanced modes” are being developed to improve efficiency and science yield. One such mode uses single actuators for electric field probing, extending the linear regime and allowing higher probe amplitudes without estimator bias. This may increase signal-to-noise, reduce exposure time, accelerate dark-hole convergence, and extend operation to stars as faint as V~5. The Coronagraph Community Participation Program’s Hardware Working Group is validating this enhancement using the cgi-howfsc control software and a PROPER-based optical model of CGI. We show simulation results where this may show faster convergence and resilience to DM nonlinearities, supporting single-actuator probing as a low-risk, high-gain improvement for Roman CGI and future missions.

Items.Authors: Ludo Bissot, Florian Quatresooz, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Claude Oestges, Olivier Absil
Items.Title: Enhancing LEO downlink performance with Model Predictive Control: a simulation study on the SALTO Telescope
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence degrades satellite to ground optical links, especially under poor conditions and fast low-Earth-orbit tracking. To reduce the temporal error, the principal limitation in such scenarios, we investigate predictive control for adaptive optics within the SALTO telescope, a Belgian test platform for compact optical communication systems. Turbulence statistics at the Redu Space Center are derived from Weather Research and Forecasting simulations. Three controllers are compared: an LQG regulator based on an AR(1) turbulence model, a linear data-driven Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOF) predictor, and a model-based reinforcement learning controller inspired by PO4AO.

Items.Authors: Daniel R. Wilkins, Artem Poliszczuk, Steven W. Allen, Eric D. Miller, Marshall W. Bautz, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Kevan Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Matthew Heine, Sven C. Herrmann, Beverly LaMarr, Peter Orel, Abigail Y. Pan, Leonid Sajkov
Items.Title: Enhancing the sensitivity of next-generation X-ray imaging detectors with artificial intelligence and advanced event reconstruction algorithms
Items.Abstract: Advanced algorithms incorporating artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) enhance the sensitivity of X-ray imaging detectors and the scientific capabilities of future X-ray missions. We report on the development of prototype algorithms designed to provide improved identification of particle-induced background events and enhanced energy reconstruction. ML algorithms can achieve a reduction of the unrejected particle background by up to 60% compared with traditional filtering methods. Moreover, with physics-motivated models of charge diffusion within the device, we find that next-generation event reconstruction algorithms can provide an improvement in the energy resolution of CCD-like detectors at event energies below 0.5keV. We present new laboratory data that demonstrates the performance of these algorithms on next-generation SiSeRO CCD devices. Together such detector and algorithm combinations can satisfy the requirements for future X-ray flagship missions.

Items.Authors: Emily Farr, Nicholas Kruczek, Kevin France, Paloma López Reyes, Juan Larruquert, John Hennessy
Items.Title: Environmental stability testing of narrowband optical coatings in the Lyman-ultraviolet: from the lab to rockets to HWO
Items.Abstract: NASA has prioritized developing optical coatings for the Lyman- and far-ultraviolet (90–200 nm) to support future missions. To advance UV optics for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), we present the latest performance measurements and environmental stability results for band-selecting filters designed for the Lyman-ultraviolet bandpass (LUV; 90–120 nm). Lyman-UV coatings can degrade during storage and integration, with humidity reducing the reflectivity of lithium-fluoride overcoated mirrors. The narrowband filters developed with the Grupo de Óptica de Láminas Delgadas (GOLD) are Lyman-α (121.6 nm) suppressing filters peaking near 105 nm (“F110M”), now being flight-tested on the FLUID sounding rocket. We present recent CU Boulder results comparing MgF₂ and AlF₃ capped and uncapped witness samples over the first year of environmental testing, and new results using a liquid polymer protective layer on LiF-overcoated samples.

Items.Authors: Filippo Ambrosino, Francesco Dazzi, Massimo Cecconi, Francesco Leone, Adriano Ghedina, Manuel Gonzalez, Héctor Ventura, Marcos Hernandez Diaz
Items.Title: e-SiFAP: a new enhanced VIS-IR ultra-fast photometer at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo
Items.Abstract: A new, complex and challenging fast photo(VIS-IR)polarimeter(VIS) has been designed for observing compact galactic and extragalactic sources, such as neutron stars and black holes, allowing for detecting sub-second variations in pulsars and gamma-ray bursts. It has been mounted and aligned on optical table in an optical laboratory of the Astronomical Observatory of Rome, ready to be delivered to the optical laboratory of the Fundación Galileo Galilei-INAF in La Palma (Canary Islands) where it will be integrated/aligned on a special optical table which be interfaced with the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo for its final alignment and first light.

Items.Authors: Marlène de Sepibus, Elena Masciadri, Camilo Weinberger, Alessio Turchi, Angel Otarola, Steffen Mieske, Christian Veillet, Sam Ragland
Items.Title: Establishing baseline models' performances for optical turbulence forecasting
Items.Abstract: Accurate forecasting of optical turbulence helps telescopes observe with maximum efficiency as performance of AO systems depends on turbulence conditions. A wide range of forecasting methods has been explored in the literature, varying in complexity, cost, and performance. To appreciate their added value, it is necessary to benchmark them against simple reference models, or baselines, that act as thresholds. In this contribution we present two such baselines and analyze their results for all main astroclimatic and atmospheric parameters at the VLT and LBT. Each method is useful for a specific typology of forecast: prevision by persistence (PP) when we forecast the temporal evolution of a parameter, and precasting (PC) when we forecast the average value of the parameter. Finally, we discuss encouraging preliminary results on estimating these thresholds for sites different from those analysed in this paper.

Items.Authors: Takaki Nakagawa, Naoto Iida, Hiroyuki Hori, Eiji Suzuki, Takeo Manome, Kiichi Kitanaka, Kentaro Yanagibashi, Kazumi Nishikawa, Masatsugu Kamiura, Daisuke Yamanaka, Yuji Ikeda, Hitoshi Tokoro, Taiki Bessho, Masahito S. Uchiyama, Sayumi Kaji, Yoshihiko Saito, Hideaki Kotake
Items.Title: Evaluation of diffraction-limited performance of a large optical antenna for cislunar optical communication system
Items.Abstract: Future Earth–Moon optical communication requires a telescope that can maintain diffraction-limited performance despite severe thermal fluctuations, radiation, and launch loads. Fine Cordierite®, developed by Kyocera, offers ultra-low CTE, high stiffness, radiation resistance, and machinability for complex structures, enabling monolithic and highly athermal optical systems. However, large monolithic telescopes made entirely of this brittle ceramic had not been realized due to the difficulty of assembling precision optical and structural components. Leveraging two decades of accumulated manufacturing and assembly expertise, Kyocera has successfully developed the first all–Fine Cordierite® telescope. This paper summarizes its design, fabrication, and optical performance.

Items.Authors: Aditya D. Dange, Roshan Tayde, Jayant Kumbhar, Yogesh Kamble, Apurva Trivedi, Mangesh Patil
Items.Title: Evolutions in the dish pointing architecture & design of the SKA Mid telescope control system
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) is an international organisation that currently building two radio telescopes. The SKA Mid frequencies telescope (SKA Mid) located in MeerKAT National Park, South Africa will consist of 197 dish antennas with observing range between 350 MHz - 15 GHz. One of the most important function of the software control system of the telescope is to accurately point the dish towards the desired location in the sky. This paper provides the evolutionary changes along with their driving factors in the architecture, design and implementation of the dish pointing functionality of the software control system.     Keywords: SKAO, Telescope, Dish antenna, Tango,

Items.Authors: Éric M. Thiébaut, Olivier Flasseur, Samuel Thé, Loïc Denis
Items.Title: Exo-planet detection with ASAP model of nuisances
Items.Abstract: In this contribution, we propose to use the ASAP family of covariance models to take into account the statistics of the residual star light and of the noise in sequences of high-contrast images. In particular, the so-called "hierarchical" ASAP model seems very well suited to account for long-range correlations in the stellar leakages. We developed a fast unsupervised algorithm to learn the ASAP model given the sequence of scientific images and to compute detection maps. Based on ROC curves, taking into account long-range correlations improve the achieved detection contrast notably near the coronagraphic mask, that is close to the host star.

Items.Authors: Gerardo Capobianco, Vladimiro Noce, Davide Loreggia, Maurizio Pancrazzi, Silvano Fineschi, Valeria Caracci, Donata Bonino, Giovanni Franchi
Items.Title: Expected performances of X and Gamma rays detectors being operated on the Moon and in the Earth Stratosphere developed within the NRRP EMM project
Items.Abstract: As part of the “Earth Moon Mars (EMM)”project, led by INAF (Instituto Nazionale di Astrofisica) in partnership with ASI (Agenzia Spaziale Italiana) and CNR (Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche) and funded under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), we are developing the Solar X Ray Moonitor (SXRM), a Moon-based instrument to monitor solar activity from the lunar surface in the energy range of 1 to 30 keV. SXRM has two main objectives: to provide alerts in case of solar storms (flares, CME) directed at the Moon –an essential feature for future permanent missions - and to deliver diagnostics about the parent events. The final delivery of the instrument is currently expected by spring of 2026 at a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 4. We have drafted the SXRM engineering and development plan aiming at realizing a space-qualified instrument.This presentation will focus on detector simulations, radiometric computations and the identification of the critical parameters.

Items.Authors: Ricardo Ortiz
Items.Title: Extending Aluminum Coating Life: In-Situ Wet Washing Results for the 2016 MMT 6.5m Primary Mirror
Items.Abstract: Wet washing the 2016 coating of the 6.5m MMT primary mirror in-situ has yielded the most recent results. By performing mirror washing once or twice a year, we’ve exceeded the expected lifespan of our coating. We’ll present a comprehensive overview of our 2016 unprotected aluminum coating. Over the years, we’ve maintained the standard aluminum coating on the MMT, on-glass mirrors, using water, soap, and cotton swabs. This approach has preserved the coating properties close to near-fresh levels without causing any visible scratches on the bare aluminum surface. We’ll share data on the lifespan of the 2016 coating using our Konica Minolta Spectrophotometer CM-600d.

Items.Authors: Yuichi Matsuda, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Naoki Kohara, Kazuhisa Mitsuda, Atsushi Noda, Yuichiro Ezoe, Naoshi Murakami, Satoshi Kikuta
Items.Title: Extremely large optical infrared space telescope with multiple diffractive optical elements
Items.Abstract: We introduce a concept study of an extremely large optical infrared space telescope. The main science mission is (1) to spatially resolve nearby exoplanets with habitable surface environment and (2) to map gaseous disk around the first stars in the early Universe. We require a spatial resolution of at least 1 micro arc-second to distinguish the ocean, land, plants, and volcano on the exoplanets at 10 persec from us. Therefore we require a telescope aperture size of at least 100 km. A combination of magnetically controlled formation flights of pico satellites and multiple diffractive optical elements, will enable us to realize such extremely large-aperture space telescope.

Items.Authors: Mary Iskakova, Kenneth Buffo, Casey DeRoo, Manel Errando, Gavin Frueh
Items.Title: Fabrication and characterization of electroactive polymer actuators for high-resolution adjustable X-ray optics
Items.Abstract: This work explores adjustable X-ray mirror technologies that use electroactive polymer films as actuators to correct figure errors in sub-millimeter-thick mirror segments. Such figure deviations can arise from fabrication defects, mounting stresses, or coating-induced strain and ultimately reduce angular resolution of the optics. We focus on the fabrication, characterization, and application of individually addressable actuator cells based on PVDF-TrFE electroactive polymer films deposited on flat silicon wafers. Electroactive polymers can deliver significant strains at low operating voltages, making them promising for correcting deformations in thin mirror shells of future X-ray telescopes.  We will present an updated fabrication procedure and associated figure changes. We have also developed strategies to identify and recover shorted cells, which we will discuss here.

Items.Authors: Hill Tailor, Brandon D. Chalifoux
Items.Title: Fabrication and metrology of glass support structural components for lightweight grazing-incidence X-ray telescope mirrors
Items.Abstract: Future lightweight, high-resolution X-ray telescope mirror modules rely on precisely engineered support structures to ensure optical alignment. This study develops two key components for flex-module assemblies: a glass support base and wedged glass spacers, each requiring sub-micron precision. Both components are fabricated using ultrafast laser-assisted chemical etching, where laser-written patterns are selectively removed in KOH. Custom path-generation software defines the base geometry to match the innermost mirror surface, and its accuracy is verified with chromatic confocal sensor. The required wedged spacers are produced through multi-cycle HF etching—an initial bulk-removal step followed by controlled dipping to form a linear wedge. Their geometric accuracy is assessed using low-coherence interferometry.

Items.Authors: Alexander Gliese, Raul E. Riveros
Items.Title: Fabrication of lightweight monocrystalline silicon mirrors for X-ray observatories
Items.Abstract: Advancing our understanding of fundamental physics depends on x-ray astronomical observations that exceed the capabilities of current spaceborne telescopes. Achieving the necessary sensitivity and imaging performance requires the development of x-ray focusing optics that are both exceptionally lightweight and high quality. At NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC), our team is pioneering innovative manufacturing methods for x-ray mirrors that address the demanding performance, fabrication, and cost needs of next-generation x-ray observatories. This paper presents an overview of our manufacturing process for high-precision x-ray mirror substrates and provides an update on recent developments.

Items.Authors: Jay K. Kueny, Joseph D. Long, Jared R. Males, Alycia J. Weinberger, Laird M. Close, Joshua Liberman, Jialin Li, Sebastiaan Haffert, Eden McEwen, Maggie Y. Kautz, Olivier Guyon, Logan Pearce, Katie M. Twitchell, Avalon Gower, Parker T. Johnson, Alexander Hedglen, Elena Tonucci, Matthijs Mars, Lauren Schatz, Miles Lucas
Items.Title: FFortissiMo: a novel JAX-based pipeline for freeform forward modeling of circumstellar disks
Items.Abstract: We introduce our efforts towards a data-driven approach for characterizing circumstellar disks with the novel, pixel-based freeform forward modeling pipeline, FFortissiMo. We developed FFortissiMo within the framework of JAX, which is a machine learning library in Python that enables efficient optimization through automatic differentiation ("autodiff") and GPU-accelerated array computations. Using on-sky visible light images of the disk around HR 4796 taken by the Magellan "extreme" Adaptive Optics instrument (MagAO-X), we demonstrate that our data-driven freeform models excel at fitting a complex dust distribution and can infer the dust scattering properties even through PSF subtraction artifacts. Since our pipeline outputs the deconvolved reconstruction of the disk, we will discuss the implications of retrieving morphological features finer than a resolution element.
